I mostly play just indie titles now because I've just got this massive level of "release fatigue" with what AAA games are nowadays. Imagine if you went to the movies and every movie was just a re-release of a previous movie -- sorry bad analogy. Anyway, I think that my point still stands in that, like movies, mainstream games have just become really boring now, and I find that the ones that do get made tend to waste my time with way too much pointless filler and hand holding. I think either because this is just easier content to make or that they feel the need to appeal to some mythical mass market.

There's just no craft to it anymore, at least with indie games you get a product that the guys that made it obviously care about it, so even if they might not have the same resources as one of the big studios they're going to come up with something interesting, rather than the same crap that has just been done to death. I mean sure it might just rely on some silly gimmick, but the thing is by the time that you've gotten sick of it the games normally over and you just move on to another title. They're also cheap, you don't have to just play the crap out of a game to justify dropping $60 on the thing like I did in my youth. It's like, yeah, I know what the next sandbox or modern military shooter game is going to be like because it's going to exactly like the last fifty of these titles that have gotten released. You're just not going see things like rhythm based dungeon crawlers or sandbox spaceship construction sets getting produced by any of the major studios.

Outside of a few exceptions I just can't find myself enthused by what has become the product of the mainstream, and this is coming from someone that used to be obsessed, for example I still own all three consoles of the last generation, as well as the one before that, and multiple retro consoles. If this industry has managed to alienate me as a consumer then they deserve to go broke, IMHO. I mean sure I'm old and maybe there are more than enough newer marks to support the industry even if they've managed to loss me as a punter, but I have the luxury of sitting down and comparing games from the 90's to the games that get released now, and it tends to pan out that the older titles are just more fun to me, That is being far less of a chore to get into but also having significantly more depth. Just the thought of having to play a modern game where you have to literally sit though a tutorial for 15 minutes on how to shoot gun makes me cringe hard.

Also this whole thing of treating games as some sort of a sport I just find to be really stupid. It's just something that I don't think I'll ever be able to understand, like speed running. The problem that I have is that I don't think that it's really about actually being better at the game than the other guy but more along the lines of finding exploits in the game that can be used to give you an advantage against the other guy. That there's really two levels of competition, one against the other dude, but this vastly different one against the game itself, or the latest meta of that. It's just a level of nerdism that I think prevents this ever being taken seriously as a sport. But I would say that being a scrub.

It is an unfortunate truth of the Internet. Everything good on the Net goes through the same cycle, and ends up in one of two places: Dead or Immortal.

The something (website, service, whatever) is created. It's usefulness causes it's userbase to grow and grow. Eventually the userbase will reach a critical mass, and the two potential outcomes come into play:

  1. Those in charge of the something will feel a false sense of importance, and begin making changes to the something that are considered terrible by the majority of the userbase, and lauded by a vocal minority. Those in charge will begin catering more and more to the vocal minority, until eventually a mass exodus occurs and the something "dies". Whether it truly dies or not is of no real importance, as it is dead for all intents and purposes to the overwhelming majority of people on the Net.

  2. Those in charge of the something realize that it has reached it's full potential, and so they sit back and allow things to continue naturally. If the function of the something proves itself truly invaluable, it will stand the test of time and become a nigh-permanent feature of the Internet. Otherwise, it's userbase will slowly dwindle as more tantalizing options are made available.

Most sites will suffer the fate in 1 because their creator(s) is/are arrogant and ignorant (Digg, 4chan, Reddit). Those that choose 2 will still most likely end in "death". A very rare few that choose 2 will prove themselves truly irreplaceable, finding themselves enshrined in the depths of the Web (Zophar's Domain, The Patches Scrolls, GameCopyWorld, The Pirate Bay).

And with each iteration the cycle picks up speed.
